The evidence on whether kinesiology taping enhances sports performance is genuinely conflicting across peer-reviewed research. Some studies report positive effects: a PMC article notes that KT has been shown to be clinically effective for "enhancing functional performance" and improving muscle activities [d2], and a study on semi-professional soccer players found that "Kinesio taping had immediate effects on improving strength, performance and balance" [d9]. However, multiple higher-quality systematic reviews and controlled studies contradict these findings. A systematic review of 15 studies concluded that "overall, KT did not produce significant effects on a wide variety of sports performance abilities" and found "a lack of compelling evidence to support the use of KT to enhance the sports performance abilities" [d12]. A peer-reviewed study on elite cyclists found that KTT "exerted no considerable effects on all physiological and kinematic measures," despite cyclists perceiving improved performance [d8]. Similarly, a BMC Sports Science study found that "kinesiology tape does not alter lower limb performance or muscle function in healthy adults" [d4], and a Semantic Scholar summary of multiple studies noted that "KT was not found to be useful in improving performance in some sports-related movements in healthy college athletes" and that "taping does not enhance power and speed in young healthy athletes" [d13]. A critical review goes further, stating that "taping certainly doesn't increase circulation, enhance performance, promote injury recovery, reduce inflammation, or provide meaningful support" [d7]. Overall, the weight of peer-reviewed evidence suggests kinesiology taping does not reliably enhance sports performance, though some individual studies in specific populations show modest benefits.
